_: NOTES-FROM-PLANNING.md entry 146: a tour of the application, one page per screen, at /tour/.
Alan: 'I think there should be a separate page for screenshots of each section of the application that explains
what is happening instead of just a few screenshots on the main page.' A handful of pictures on the home page
shows that GroupLab exists. It does not show what using it is like, and that is the question somebody has before
This file is the list. website/build.py builds the index and one page per screen from it, and refuses to build if
a screen here has no screenshot or a screenshot has no screen here, so the tour and the weekly screenshot job of
entry 144 section 4 cannot drift apart quietly.
Every 'part' must name something a reader can actually see in the picture, in the words the screen itself uses.
No class names, no file paths, and nothing claimed that is not in the build the pictures came from.
Entry 152: what each screen does with a target GroupLab did not print is a field of its own, 'withoutASheet',
and every screen has one. On several of them the honest answer is 'no difference', and saying so is worth a line.
docs/WHAT-CAN-BE-MEASURED.md is the one source for what GroupLab can measure and where the scale comes from;
nothing here states its own version of that.
Entry 155: the Target library and Printing were two screens doing one job, and are one screen now, Targets. /tour/library/ and
/tour/print/ are each a plain page with one link to /tour/targets/, since entry 151 bans a meta refresh, so a link to either still arrives.

firstrun.name: The first run
firstrun.blurb: The first time GroupLab opens it asks, one question at a time, whether your scope is in mil or MOA, then three more: whether to send your targets, whether to send error reports, and whether to take part in the hardware survey.
firstrun.purpose: GroupLab works in your scope's unit from the start, and nothing leaves your computer until you have said it may. Each sharing question says exactly what would be sent before you answer it, and each has a way to say no. The answers are kept and can be changed at any time in Settings, under Units and Sharing.
firstrun.withoutASheet: No difference. It appears before any sheet is opened.
parts: Question 2 of 4
Where you are, over a bar with one part for each question: the one showing in amber, those answered in teal.
Send your targets
What goes with each target, then the two consents, testing only or may be published, and the answers: send everything you open, send finished targets only, ask me each time, or never.
Back, Skip for now and Next
Back returns to the question before. Skip for now moves on and records nothing, so that question is asked again the next time GroupLab starts. Next passes over a question already answered.
The other questions

Is your scope in mil or MOA? comes first, with whether sizes on the paper are in inches or millimeters; after sending targets come error reports, what a report holds and what it never holds, and the hardware survey, whose Yes does not run the benchmark.
steps: Open GroupLab for the first time.
Say whether your scope is in mil or MOA, and whether you measure in inches or millimeters.
Read each sharing question and answer it; No is always one of the answers, and Skip for now leaves one for the next start.
Change any answer later in Settings, under Units and Sharing.
firstrun.fits: Shown once, over the marking screen, before anything else, one question at a time.

marking.name: Marking and review
marking.blurb: Every hole found and numbered to its bull, with anything uncertain raised for you to settle.
marking.purpose: This is where GroupLab shows its working before it measures anything. It finds the holes, works out the scale from the printed markers, and assigns each hole to a bull. Where it is not sure, it says so and asks, rather than quietly guessing and giving you a clean-looking number built on a guess. On a target GroupLab did not print, any target you already shoot, this is where you set the scale once and mark the holes by hand, and the same statistics follow.
marking.withoutASheet: The same screen, and the work is yours. You set the scale, by tapping a known length or the corners of a known rectangle, which removes the photograph's angle, and you place each shot. On a target with several bulls, the bulls tool places each bull's aim point: shots go to their nearest bull and are drawn in its color, the lasso moves several at once to another, and a length drawn near a bull can be that bull's own scale, so an angled photograph is measured right at every bull; the bulls can be kept as a template for the next sheet of the same target. That was Unholy's suggestion (also TNA). There is no automatic detection, and the review queue stays empty, because it exists to question what the detector decided and nothing decided anything.
parts: The tabs across the top

Each target open has its own tab: its name, Analysis or Marking, and a dot that turns amber while it has marks that are not saved. The + tab opens another target, Ctrl+Tab moves between them, and each keeps its own marks and zoom. Closing a tab with unsaved marks asks first.
Setup, at the top of the panel

Caliber, shot distance and rounds fired come first, each saying in a line what it unlocks. One that matters and is still empty is outlined and says needed, until you answer it or say not known. Rifle and barrel are one list, with the barrel on now first, then the load. The paper and the backing wait at the bottom in a closed fold, For the hole size studies, which records them only, changes no detection and is remembered for the next sheet.
The count at the top
How many shots are marked and how many need review, so you know how much is left before you can trust the result.
Review, on the right

One question at a time, in order, each saying what GroupLab thinks and why. The buttons are the answers. Here it has found 24 marks on a sheet that takes 25, nobody has said how many rounds were fired, and it has put its best candidate first with the evidence for it.
Which bull each shot belongs to

A thin line runs from every hole to its bull, and Lines to bulls switches them off. A line worth a second look is dashed in orange with a question mark beside the hole, and Next unsure hole goes to the next one. Click a bull to choose it: it gets a blue ring, its lines turn blue, the others fade, and clicking holes gives them to it or takes them away until you press Done or Escape.
The numbers on the picture

Each bull's number stands in plain gray at the top left, outside its ring, and each hole's number in a dark tag just outside the ring, where it covers no other number and no hole. Several holes on one bull have their tags in a column beside it on short lines. The shot you select is an open magenta ring with four short ticks, so the hole stays in sight, and its tag turns magenta.
How did you shoot this sheet?

Three cards: one shot on each bull I used, some bulls took two or more (then tap those bulls), or every hole to its nearest bull. Bulls left blank are found by themselves, with buttons to tap the ones that took two or the ones you fired at. Loads on this sheet sets one load, one a row, one a column, or the bulls you pick, and a line reads back what GroupLab will make of it.
The numbered list underneath
Every question still to answer, the current one marked NOW and the next marked NEXT.
The keyboard line

C pans and V selects, side by side under the left hand. Space moves to the next item, Enter takes the first choice, a bull's number reassigns the selected shot, N marks it not a hole. Faster than the mouse once a sheet has a dozen questions.
Selected shot

Everything known about the one you have picked: where it is, how wide the hole is, how many holes' worth of ink it contains, and how far it is from anything else. The three chips say whether it was detected, corrected by you, or added by hand.
Called flyer and Counted

Marking a shot you called as a flyer, or turning Counted off to leave it out of the measurement, which asks no reason. GroupLab keeps it on the sheet and says so in the analysis rather than deleting it; a reason stored earlier is shown, read only. Delete, not a hole takes a staple or a tear away, and Remove the mark deletes it fully.
Scale

Which markers gave the scale and how many of them were read, and for a photograph how far off square it was and how good it is. This is what makes the measurement real, so it is shown rather than assumed.
Find the paper's edges

With the rectangle tool, on a target GroupLab did not print: the paper's four corners placed for you when the sheet stands out from what is behind it, and a standard paper size offered when the photograph's shape matches one.
The tools along the top of the picture

Pan, which is the tool on open and also selects a mark you click without moving it, then measure, box, the scale ends, the bull picker, and select, which is the one that drags a mark. Undo and redo sit beside them.
Detect on a GroupLab sheet
Runs the detection again, for instance after you have entered the caliber.
Accept and analyze
When you are satisfied. It saves the session and takes you to the analysis.
steps: Open your photograph or scan, by dragging it onto the window or from the file menu.
Answer the setup at the top: the caliber, the distance and how many rounds you fired, or say not known.
Answer each review item in turn, using the buttons or the keys shown.
Drag any mark that sits off a hole with the select tool, V, and use a bull's number to move a shot to the right bull.
Mark anything you called as a flyer, then press Accept and analyze.

analysis.name: The analysis
analysis.blurb: Every shot on one bull, with the six figures a shooter reads in view and everything else one click away.
analysis.purpose: Twenty-five bulls shot one round each become one picture of twenty-five shots, because each shot is measured from its own bull. Every number here comes with an interval, which is the range the true value could really be given how few shots you fired. That is the difference between knowing a load is better and hoping it is. Tap any number to switch its units: angles between mil and MOA, sizes between inches and centimeters, and GroupLab remembers it for that figure.
analysis.withoutASheet: No difference. Every figure here is worked out from the marks and the scale, and it does not matter whether a detector placed them or you did.
parts: Back, top left
Returns to marking with every edit as you left it.
The composite, in the middle

A dot at each shot's center, drawn where it landed relative to its own bull, on white with dark outlines at the hole size, so it reads on a laptop in daylight. The group center and the extreme spread line are the one color that stands out.
The key, under the plot

In a compact box directly under the plot, in two columns where it fits, so it never covers a shot: what each mark means, listing only what is shown: the shots, the red extreme spread line, the green CEP circles (50 dotted, 90 solid, 95 dashed), the green lines through the group center and the blue lines through where you aimed, and, where the session has chronograph readings, the amber velocity band. A shot you pick is ringed, with a cross through it, in a magenta nothing else uses, over everything else. Toggles beside the plot turn CEP 50, 90 and 95, the extreme spread and the velocity band on and off, and Group or Whole target frames the group alone or the entire bull; GroupLab remembers both. The wheel or a pinch zooms, dragging empty paper moves the view, and a double click fits it again.
Zero correction

How far the group center is from where you aimed, across and up and down, on the paper and in your scope's unit, mil or MOA, the rifle's where the session names one, and the distance the correction is for. Beneath it one line says what to dial, in clicks of your scope with the click value, or that the offset cannot yet be told from chance. Its why holds the give or take. Zero from this group opens the same in a window, with how well the center is known, and carries the offset into Ballistics.
Group

Center from aim, extreme spread, group width by height, mean radius, and CEP 50 and 90. With the shot distance set each is an angle first, in your scope's unit, mil or MOA, with its size on the paper beneath; without it, the size on the paper and a button to set the distance. Hover over a figure for the range it could really be and the figure without any shot you left out.
Velocity and the vertical

How much of the group's up-and-down spread comes from velocity alone, from the session's chronograph readings and the load's BC at the distance shot: the share in amber with its range, a meter from none to all of it, and the measured vertical spread beside what velocity alone would make. Where each reading was paired with its shot, a chart of height against velocity says whether the shots follow the solver. Without readings it says what they add and offers Import a file, Type them in (speeds in the order fired, then Match to shots) and a place to drop a chronograph's file; without the distance or the BC it says which is missing, with a button to it; where the range reaches all of the spread it says the data cannot tell.
Advanced, closed until you open it

Sigma, the strips across and up and down, the order fired, the shape and flyer tests, the full CEP table, sighters, and carrying the correction to another distance. GroupLab remembers whether you opened it.
The scale badge

At the top of the figures: Scale checked, with a tick, when the sheet's own markers set the scale, and a line under it saying how the scale was found, from the printed markers with your printer check or the scan's resolution behind them, a length you measured, or a store-bought target's printed size. The detail is behind Show work.
The load block, left
Which rifle, barrel, load and caliber this sheet was shot with, and where the caliber came from.
Shots, from their own bull

Every shot as numbers, across, up and down, and radius, each heading naming its unit (across, in), following the length unit chosen in Settings. The shot you pick on the plot or the picture has an amber bar down its row, a brighter row and bold numbers, and the table scrolls to it; clicking the red dashed line picks the widest pair. Shots and clicks beneath it lists each shot as a short row; open one to change its bull, say its place in the firing order, turn Counted off or choose Delete, not a hole. Share a picture puts a results box and the mean radius circle on the photograph.
Own window, Show work, Report and Export

Own window moves the figures to a window of their own for a second monitor. Show work opens how the sheet was read. Report makes the full report or a one-page report. Export writes the complete record, or the shot coordinates as CSV for a spreadsheet.
steps: Read the mean radius, and hover over it for the range it could really be.
Check the zero correction and the line under it saying what to dial, or that the offset is not real yet at this many shots.
Open Advanced for the strips across and up and down, and the tests.
Report or Export if you want to keep it outside GroupLab.

analysis-open.name: Showing the work
analysis-open.blurb: The same analysis with every explanation opened, so no number on the screen is one you have to take on trust.
analysis-open.purpose: Every figure GroupLab shows has a why beside it. This is the analysis with all of them open at once. It exists because a measurement you cannot check is a measurement you cannot argue with, and the whole point of measuring a group is to settle an argument about a load.
analysis-open.withoutASheet: No difference. The explanations are of the arithmetic, which is the same either way, except that the scale is named as the one you set.
parts: The why links
Beside every figure on the analysis. Each opens the reasoning for that one number: what was measured, over how many shots, and what the interval means.
Show work, at the top
Opens all of them together, which is this view.
The review notice
Where decisions were left unmade in marking, it says how many and offers to take you back to them, because an analysis over unsettled marks is worth less than one over settled ones.
Shots Needed to Zero

Under the full CEP table: how many shots a zeroing group needs to land on the closest click, or within one click, 90, 95 and 99 times in 100, from the group's spread and your scope's click value. Suggested by Jylee.
steps: Press Show work on the analysis.
Read the reasoning beside any number you are about to act on.
Press it again to fold them away.

sessions.name: Session records
sessions.blurb: Every sheet you have accepted, newest first, ready to open again or to compare.
sessions.purpose: A session is one sheet, accepted and saved. This is the list of them. It is how you go back to a result weeks later, and how you pick which two loads to put side by side.
sessions.withoutASheet: No difference. A session from a hand-marked target is saved, listed and reopened like any other.
parts: Rifle and Load
Narrow the list to one rifle or one load. Choosing a single load also shows whether it is getting better or worse over time.
The tick boxes
Choose two or more sessions to compare.
The columns
Date, sheet, rifle, load, distance, how many shots, and the mean radius with its interval, so you can see at a glance which sessions are worth comparing without opening any of them.
Compare the chosen
Takes the ticked sessions to the compare screen.
A row
Opens that session's analysis again, exactly as it was.
Delete
Removes one session. It does not touch the image it was made from.
steps: Filter by rifle or load if the list is long.
Tick the sessions you want to put beside each other.
Press Compare the chosen, or click a row to reopen its analysis.
sessions.fits: Filled by the analysis every time you accept a sheet. Feeds compare loads.

compare.name: Compare loads
compare.blurb: Two or more sessions side by side, and a plain sentence saying whether the shots actually tell them apart.
compare.purpose: This is the screen that answers the question load development is for. It puts the groups beside each other, then draws each measurement as the range it could really be. Where those ranges overlap, the shots have not told the loads apart, and it says so in words rather than leaving you to read it off a chart.
compare.withoutASheet: No difference, with one thing worth knowing: a hand-set scale that assumes a square-on photograph carries that assumption into the comparison, and the figures say so.
parts: The plots along the top

One per load. Dots are the shots about their own bulls, excluded ones left out, each load in its own color with a dashed circle around its group. Tap a group to stack them on one center. With two loads, What the difference means fills the rest of the card: each load's shots, mean radius, extreme spread and CEP 90 side by side, whether these shots can tell the two apart, and how many shots each would take to tell a 10 percent difference apart. The article linked below shows what two real sheets compared can say.
The figures under each plot
Sigma, mean radius and extreme spread, with the range each could really be where one is given.
Mean radius, with the range each could really be

Each load's name on a line of its own, and under it a line showing the whole interval with the measured value marked on it and written at the right. Two lines that overlap are two loads these shots cannot separate.
The sentence underneath

The conclusion in plain words, and never one the verdict below disagrees with. Here: every one of these overlaps every other, so these shots do not tell them apart by this figure; where they group is another matter, in the card below.
Sigma, with the range each could really be
The same treatment for the other measure of spread.
The header
How many loads, how many shots in total, and that they are in the order you chose.
steps: Tick two or more sessions in session records and press Compare the chosen.
Read the sentence under the mean radius bars before you read the numbers.
If the intervals overlap, shoot more of both loads rather than picking a winner.
Look at the plots for a difference in shape that the single numbers hide.
compare.fits: From session records. It is usually where a load development session ends.

equipment.name: Equipment
equipment.blurb: Your rifles, barrels and loads. A sheet names one of each, and everything else takes what it needs from here.
equipment.purpose: Rather than typing the same rifle into every session, you record it once. Everything is optional except a name: GroupLab will happily measure a group for a rifle it knows nothing else about. The extra fields are there because the ballistics page and the zero correction need them, and it says which one is missing when it cannot work something out.
equipment.withoutASheet: No difference. Nothing here depends on a sheet.

Two tabs. A session names a rifle with its barrel, and a load.
The list on the left

Name is the only field you must fill in. Sight height and Zeroed at are the two the zero correction uses; scope and click value matter for the ballistics page. A Scope and mount part on the rifle form holds the elevation travel of the scope, the rail cant, a sight scale factor and the weight as fired; it shows what the scope and mount allow and sets the Top Gun trend from Bryan Litz beside each load.
Barrels on this rifle

A table under the rifle: the barrel that is on now (a radio button), its name, length, twist, direction and rounds, Edit, and Add a barrel. The rifle takes its length and twist from the barrel on now. Barrels from earlier versions were moved under their rifles; any it could not place wait under a rifle named Barrels not yet on a rifle.
Notes
Anything that does not fit a field. It travels with the record.
The line along the bottom
A reminder that nothing here changes a marking. A sheet names which of these it was shot with, and that is all.

ballistics.name: Ballistics
ballistics.blurb: A trajectory for one rifle and load, a dope table at whatever spacing you ask for, the chance of a hit from your own measured precision, and Point blank, the range you can hold dead on.
ballistics.purpose: Everything else in GroupLab measures what your rifle did. This works out what it should do. It takes the rifle and load you have already recorded, asks for the air it will be shot in, and gives you drop, wind drift, velocity and energy out to whatever distance you name, and the chance of a hit there from your own measured precision. Nothing here changes a marking or an analysis.
ballistics.withoutASheet: No difference. Nothing here depends on a sheet.
parts: Along the top
The rifle and load, chosen from what you recorded on the equipment screen, Imperial or metric, and the one amber button: Work out the table, or Work out the chance in the hit probability view.
The rifle, The load, The air, The table

The settings on the left, in sections that fold and say what they hold in one line when folded. GroupLab remembers which you left open. A field the solver still needs says needed beside it, and its section opens.
Keep these on the records
Writes what you have typed back to the rifle and load, so you do not type it again.
Trajectory, Hit probability or Point blank
The three views of the middle, chosen at its top and remembered.
Drop, Wind drift, Velocity, Energy
Four views of the same trajectory on a large chart. It marks your zero and the range chosen on the right; clicking a point chooses it.
Dope table
Drop, elevation and clicks, the drift of a 10 mph wind, velocity and energy at every step. Clicking a row chooses that range, and its row is highlighted.
At one range

The right column: the elevation for one range in large amber figures with its clicks and drop, then the wind, velocity, energy, time of flight and stability. Stability says what it needs when the twist is empty.
The analyzed group there
The group open in the analysis carried through the solver to that range, labeled a prediction, with its sigma there and its interval.
The target, What you are unsure of

The hit probability view's settings: the target, its distance, which is the range on the right, and where the precision comes from; then a confidence preset for everything nobody can measure, with each figure and a bias beside it for something you know is off.
Hit probability
A card that leads with the first round's chance and its interval, then the second round, corrected from the first, beside the simulated first rounds drawn on the target.
Point blank

The third view of the middle: from your mean radius and a certainty, how far you can hold dead on at a chosen animal or target, how to set the zero for it in clicks, and a card to print. The rifle, load and air are the ones already chosen.
What costs the most
Every error source by the hits it takes away, largest first with a bar for each, so you can see whether the wind call, the load or the range estimate is what to work on.
The shot and the simulation
Folded until you want it: the shot angle, latitude and direction of fire, and the trials and seed that make a result repeatable.
steps: Choose the rifle and load along the top.

Set the air, or leave the pressure empty and give the altitude.
Set the distance and step, press Work out the table, and click a row or a point on the chart to see that range on the right.
For a hit probability, switch the middle to Hit probability, set the target, choose the confidence preset closest to your situation, and press Work out the chance.

settings.name: Settings
settings.blurb: Eight categories down the left, a search box above them, and one page at a time. Every choice here is remembered as soon as it is made.
settings.purpose: Settings is a menu of eight categories, General, Units and figures, Shooting defaults, Printers and paper, Sync and your data, Sharing and privacy, Updates and about, and Help and problems, with Find a setting at its top and the chosen page on the right. Each page is cards of rows, the name on the left and its control on the right, and ends with Put this page back as it came, which asks first and puts back only that page's choices, never your records. Settings opens at the page you left it on.
settings.withoutASheet: No difference. Nothing here depends on a sheet.
parts: Find a setting
Finds rows by their names, their lines of help and other words for them, such as metric, MOA, dark or backup, and shows them on every page at once, each under its page's name.
General
The theme; the text size, Normal, Larger or Largest, with nothing cut off at any size; Reduce motion, following the system, on or off; the guided demo; and Reset layout.
Units and figures

The scope unit first, mil or MOA, then lengths and distances. Displayed only; nothing stored changes. Then the size on the paper first, what the caliber box offers, whether the analysis opens with the main figures or every figure, and what the zero correction says of an axis inside the scatter.
Shooting defaults

What a new target starts with: the last distance or always one you choose, rounds fired asked for, one a bull or not known, and the last rifle and load or none. The caliber is still asked for every target.
Printers and paper

Every printer you have checked, how large it prints across and down and when it was measured, the one photographs are corrected by, Check again, Printer calibrated or serviced and Add a printer; and Letter or A4 for GroupLab's own sheets.
Sync and your data
A daily copy of your records, the newest 14 kept, with Back up now and Restore a copy; Sync between devices; how a target is saved; and Export all my data and Import data, which overwrites nothing.
Sharing and privacy

The three things GroupLab may send, in the first run screen's order and words: targets, error reports and the hardware survey, each with its choice, one short line, and More for exactly what it sends. Nothing goes unless you chose it.
Updates and about
Which train to follow and how often to check, this build's version and commit to copy into a bug report, a link to the project's source, and Support GroupLab.
Help and problems
Report a problem, detailed logging and where the log is, and any crash records not yet dealt with.

targets.name: Targets
targets.blurb: The {count:sheets} sheets GroupLab comes with and any you design, grouped by what they are for, and everything it takes to print the one you choose, on one screen.
targets.merged: This was two screens, the target library and printing. They did the same job, so they are one screen now.
targets.purpose: This is where you choose which sheet to print and print it. Every sheet is designed for a particular job at a particular distance, and the description under each says which. A GroupLab sheet is the easy path, because it carries its own scale, its own orientation and the positions of its bulls in the markers printed around them, so nothing has to be set by hand. It prints at its true size. A sheet printed smaller than it should be is still read correctly, bull by bull, because the markers shrank with everything else. It matters for photographs, because a photograph cannot measure the print scale; a scan can and corrects for it. A scan measures the scale and reports every size in real inches; a photograph of a sheet printed at 97 percent makes every group read about 3 percent large. For real inches from a photograph, scan one sheet or measure one ruler distance, once per printer; GroupLab remembers it. So this screen asks the PDF viewer for no scaling, prints the instruction along the bottom of the sheet so you can check with a ruler, and refuses outright when the paper cannot hold the sheet. Scale markers, folded under their own heading, print the corner brackets, scale bars and board stickers that let GroupLab take the scale from a photo of a target it did not print, and measure a board once.
targets.withoutASheet: Nothing on this screen applies. It holds and prints GroupLab's own sheets; a target from anywhere else is opened on the marking screen instead.
parts: The list, grouped by what the sheet is for

Centerfire load development, rimfire, large format, long range on tiled pages, long range on roll media, and zeroing grids. A zeroing grid is for sighting in by eye at the bench, read off the grid after each shot, and says on the sheet what its squares are, with a ruler to check the print; for a zero worked out from a group, and group figures, use a 5x5 sheet. The 2 MOA sheets, requested by Unholy, are under centerfire load development: nine 2.00 in bulls on a page, one page for a quick group or a zero check, or a set of three pages for load development that GroupLab pools and that says which page is missing. The right hand column of each row is the paper size and how many scoring bulls it has, with the sighter bulls after the plus sign. The zeroing grids are design C3, chosen by Alan with Jylee and Unholy: a square and a tick of your scope's own, the numbers outside the grid.
The sheet you have chosen, beside the list
Its name and full description: the bull spacing, the sighter row, the distance it was designed for, and the paper it wants. Choosing a sheet fills everything under it at once.
Bulls in black, blue or red
Any sheet's bulls, rings and numbers in black, blue or red, remembered for that sheet; the codes, markers, title and load block stay black, and large solid areas print as a lighter tint.
Built in and read only
The sheets that come with GroupLab cannot be edited. Duplicate makes a copy that is yours, to rename and change.
The load block
Blank, to write on at the range, or filled in now from its fields.
Print the actual-size instruction
Adds a line along the bottom edge of each sheet telling whoever prints it to choose Actual size and never Fit. Leave it on unless you are printing for yourself and know the driver.
Label targets and thermal printers

Six-bull labels on 4x6, A6 and 100 by 150 mm, in sets of five that pool, and a printer check label. With a thermal printer chosen under Print on, the preview shows every dot as it will print, in black only. No label printer has been tested yet: until one prints GroupLab's check page, it should work but is not proven.
Open to print, Save PDF and Print
Open to print hands the PDF to your usual viewer, which is the safest route today. Save PDF writes the file. Print goes straight to a driver, on Windows.
Print a volunteer pack
The sheet plus one page telling somebody else how to shoot it, photograph it and send it back.
Previous sheet, Next sheet

For a tiled sheet that spans several pages. The counter says which page of how many. A tiled sheet can also be printed on one large page with cut lines between the sheets, for a plotter; each piece scans on its own.
The preview, with Zoom in, Zoom out, Fit and Open as PDF

The page about to print, drawn live from the same shapes and letters its PDF is written from, filling the rest of the screen: it changes the moment any setting does, words included, and stays sharp however far you go in on any screen. Open as PDF opens the real PDF in your viewer.
Design your own sheet

For a sheet no built-in one covers. The designer opens beside the list, and your own sheets appear at the bottom of it. At its top, made for your optic: give the distance, the lowest magnification you will shoot at, or a red dot's size, and the shots, and GroupLab sizes a bull you can center on through it and makes as many sheets as the shots need.
steps: Find the group that matches what you are doing: load development, rimfire, zeroing.

Measure one printed bull with a ruler against the size in the description before you shoot a whole session on it.

optic.name: Made for your optic
optic.blurb: Say how far, the lowest magnification you shoot at, or a red dot's size, and how many shots, and GroupLab draws a sheet whose bulls you can center on through that optic.
optic.purpose: A bull you cannot see the middle of is a bull you cannot aim at the same way twice, and that is what spreads a group before the rifle does. The aim point test of 2026-09-26 found that a feature needs about {optic:arcminutes} arcminutes at the lowest magnification a sheet is shot at before it can be centered on. So GroupLab draws a black disc with a white center of that size at the distance you give, and a small dot in the middle, nothing thinner, because a crosshair covered the thin cross and the open gap in that test. Through a red dot, whose dot hides whatever is under it, the white center is {optic:dotMargin} times the dot. At 100 yards through 10x the white center comes out {optic:at10x.centerInches} inches across in a disc of {optic:at10x.discInches}, {optic:at10x.bullsPerSheet} bulls {optic:at10x.pitchInches} inches apart on one Letter sheet for 25 shots. Through 4x it is {optic:at4x.centerInches} inches in a disc of {optic:at4x.discInches}, so only {optic:at4x.bullsPerSheet} bulls fit a sheet and 25 shots take {optic:at4x.sheets} sheets, each of which names itself by its codes.
optic.withoutASheet: Nothing here reads a target. It draws a GroupLab sheet to print, which then reads itself like every other.
parts: What you enter
The distance in yards; the lowest magnification you will shoot at, 1 for a red dot, with the dot's size in MOA; and how many shots. Make the sheet draws it.
Why it is that size
Under the button GroupLab says what it drew and why, in the sentences the picture shows: the feature size at your magnification, the disc and its center, and how many bulls fit how many sheets.
The sheet
On the right, the sheet itself, as it will print. The column in the middle still names the sheet chosen in the list; the preview is the one just made.
Printing it
It prints like any sheet, at its true size, and Save to your own sheets keeps it in your own sheets beside the built-in ones.

fingerprint.name: Add a store-bought target
fingerprint.blurb: A target GroupLab does not know yet, photographed blank and turned into a small fingerprint file in five steps, one question at a time, to send so a later GroupLab recognizes it.
fingerprint.purpose: GroupLab names a few store-bought targets by themselves and takes their scale from their printed size. Every other one has to be taught, and teaching it means a fingerprint: the features of its printing, its layout, its size and where its bulls are, made from a photograph of a blank one. These steps make it. The photo is read for the target's four corners; one true length sets the scale, from the printed size on the package, a GroupLab sheet laid on the target, or two points a measured distance apart; the target is straightened; you confirm its bulls; and you name it and save the file. The file holds the fingerprint, the name, the size and the bulls, never the photo, and each one sent is checked by hand before it joins the library a later GroupLab recognizes. Markers in the photo, corner brackets, a scale bar or a measured board's stickers, are chosen by themselves when they are found, and a bank card is one more choice, blanked out of the photo at once.
fingerprint.withoutASheet: This screen is for targets GroupLab did not print. It never reads a GroupLab sheet as the target; a GroupLab sheet in the photo is only a ruler for the scale.
fingerprint.fits: Before you shoot a target GroupLab does not know. Once a later build carries its fingerprint, a photo of it shot is named, its bulls placed and its scale set, as nine store-bought targets, from Birchwood Casey and the National Target Company, are now.
parts: The steps on the left
Photo, Size and scale, Straighten, The bulls, and Name and send: done steps ticked in teal, the one you are on in amber.
The photo in the middle

The target the way up it was taken, its outline found from the paper's edges and color and its four corners as amber handles to drag where one is off. Scroll or pinch to zoom; while a corner is dragged a magnifier above it shows the point under the finger, and a corner let go lands on the clear corner nearest it, with Undo.
Rotate left and Rotate right

On the Photo and Straighten steps, a quarter turn for a photo taken sideways or one whose camera did not say which way up it was; R and Shift R do the same on the computer. The corners are looked for again on the turned picture.
How big is this target?

Ways to give one true length: markers found in the photo, its printed size, with width and height boxes, a GroupLab sheet in the photo, two points and a distance, or a bank card beside it. Under the one picked, what GroupLab measured for that way on test photos, never a promise that one is always best.
Back and Next
Back keeps what you did; Next names where it goes, and on the last step becomes Save reference file.
